source.title: Engineering Monosemanticity in Toy Models
source.authors: A. Jermyn; Nicholas Schiefer; Evan Hubinger

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. There are minor text-extraction and formatting artifacts, but no material section appears cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures monosemanticity in toy networks and tests how it changes with model width and training choices, using a different setting and measure from the modern-model audit claims.
record.gate_note: The study tests synthetic toy networks on feature-decoding, re-projector and absolute-value tasks; it does not test language-model neuron explanations on held-out activations. Figures comparing training conditions are included only where the paper also states an outcome in text. No row is included for sparsity's loss cost alone because the paper does not report a monosemanticity outcome for that comparison.
record.test_reason: In synthetic two-layer toy networks with known features, the study measures how training path (initial bias, learning rate, weight decay), activation function and width change neuron monosemanticity at equal loss. This bears on V4's core idea that polysemanticity comes from training and architecture choices rather than capacity. It is a new, much simpler setting than V4's vision and language models, so it is T3, not T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that, with feature-sparse inputs, toy models can be made more monosemantic at no loss cost by changing which minimum training finds, using moderate negative biases. Wider layers yield more monosemantic neurons at higher compute cost, and naive weight sparsity degraded performance. The method is fragile because it depends on the bias decay rate. They do not understand the algorithm of the most polysemantic models.
record.recipe_differences: Synthetic two-layer toy networks with known features; measures neuron responses to single-feature inputs rather than testing natural-language neuron explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Monosemanticity changes with layer width, learning rate, initial bias and bias weight decay, activation function, task, and feature frequency.
record.problems: Synthetic tasks and known feature distributions limit transfer to modern language or vision models. The monosemanticity threshold is chosen by the authors (ri > 0.999). No uncertainty estimates are stated, and the authors did not analyze their most-polysemantic models mechanistically.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted under the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: All of it; no Qwen3-32B or neuron-pole audit.
All of it; no language models, mixture-of-experts models or large-scale models.
All of it; no InceptionV1 or cat/car neuron analysis.
Real vision or language models, late layers, interpretability-tool quality, modern architectures, and the essay's 5%→99% estimates for InceptionV1-sized models.
All of it; no attribution graphs.
All of it; no explanations from activating examples.
All of it; no automated simulation scoring.

missing.what: Comparison with L1 activation regularization: negative-bias training matched the best L1 model's monosemanticity at comparable or lower loss. Bears on V4's regularization point.

Even highly monosemantic engineered models keep about d+1 (65 at d=64) polysemantic neurons, which implement a low-rank identity map. A residual polysemantic share remains whatever the training choice.
Power-law feature-frequency replication of the learning-rate and negative-bias results.

record.verdict_notes: Applying V4 to toy networks is a stretch: V4 concerns real vision and language models and interpretability tools. The verdicts therefore bear only on the mechanism claim that polysemanticity is not forced by capacity. The monosemanticity threshold (ri > 0.999) is arbitrary, and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or audit of neuron poles.
No language models, dense-versus-MoE comparison, or scaling to large parameter counts.
No InceptionV1 neurons, cat-and-car example, or pose/recursive-generalization analysis.
Tests width and training choices in synthetic toy networks, not Inception-sized vision models, modern architectures, interpretability tools, or the essay's 5%-to-about-99% estimates.
No attribution graphs or test of whether model behavior can be reconstructed from its neurons.
Does not test explanations against activations withheld from the explanation-writing process.
No automated scoring of neuron explanations on new text.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy model
rows.operation_detail: Measured neuron monosemanticity for models trained with different learning rates and zero initial mean bias.
rows.measure: Number of features assigned one monosemantic neuron, plus assignments with two or mostly-monosemantic neurons.
rows.value: 503/512 features had one monosemantic neuron; 5 had two; the remaining 4 had mostly-monosemantic neurons with 0.9 < ri < 0.999.
rows.note: The authors say models at different learning rates had very different monosemanticity despite achieving the same loss. This is a toy-model result, not an audit of explanations.
rows.check: Baseline should be the lower-learning-rate zero-bias models in batch LR1 (e.g. LR 0.001), which reach the same loss but are largely polysemantic (Fig. 3–4). The 503/512 figure describes only the highest-LR model.

source_check.locator_found: Sec 4.1.1, Fig 3 text (503/512 for the highest-LR model); Fig 4 caption and panels: LR1 final models at LR 0.001, 0.005, 0.03
source_check.problem: The LR 0.03 is not stated next to 503/512. It matches the highest LR1 model shown in Fig 4, so the condition holds.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy model
rows.operation_detail: Initialized biases negatively and used bias-only weight decay during training to steer optimization toward monosemantic solutions.

conditions.value: bias weight decay; decay disabled for final 50% of steps

rows.measure: Fraction of neurons that were monosemantic and monosemantic neurons per feature.
rows.value: 30–50% of neurons were monosemantic, with 0.6–1 monosemantic neuron per feature.
rows.note: The result is reported for the stated initial-bias range and toy feature-decoder setup.
rows.check: Baseline should be the more positive initial biases above about -ε^1/2, where monosemantic counts drop sharply (Fig. 8–9). The 30–50% share is of all neurons at k=1024 > N, so it is not comparable to V4's shares.

source_check.locator_found: Sec 4.1.2, Fig 8 discussion: 30-50% of neurons monosemantic, 0.6-1 per feature; decay off for final 50% of steps

rows.subject: feature decoder toy model
rows.size_stated: N=512 features; d=64; k varied from 16 to 2048
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of nonlinear-layer neurons and measured monosemanticity.

conditions.value: zero and negative initial mean bias

rows.measure: Number and fraction of monosemantic neurons as a function of layer width.
rows.value: The number of monosemantic neurons increased with neuron count; the fraction of neurons that were monosemantic peaked when there was one neuron per feature.
rows.note: The authors describe an increase in absolute monosemantic-neuron count, but the fraction does not increase monotonically across widths.
rows.check: Against V4's 'not capacity' claim, width matters: monosemantic count rises with k. The authors weakly say polysemanticity is how models cope with too few neurons. However, negative-bias models are largely monosemantic at no loss cost even when k < N. Baseline should be the zero-bias batch K0.

rows.subject: feature decoder toy model
rows.operation_detail: Measured monosemanticity while varying feature frequency.
rows.measure: Fraction and number of monosemantic neurons.
rows.value: As feature frequency increased, models became more polysemantic; by Nε≈2d there were almost no monosemantic neurons.
rows.note: This shows sensitivity to the synthetic input distribution; the paper describes a smooth transition rather than a sharp phase transition.
rows.check: Dense features (Nε > d) force polysemanticity whatever the training choice, which is a representational-capacity limit. The row correctly records it but should state the baseline of ε = 1/64 or about 2^-5, where monosemanticity peaks.

source_check.locator_found: Sec 4.1.5: transition begins near Nε=d/4; almost none left by Nε≈2d; smooth, no sharp transition

rows.subject: feature decoder toy model
rows.operation_detail: Used negative initial mean bias and bias weight decay with GeLU activations, varying initial bias and learning rate.

conditions.value: approximately -1 gave a peak in monosemanticity

rows.measure: Fraction of monosemantic neurons and monosemantic neurons per feature.
rows.value: The paper reports that the approach worked with GeLU and that monosemanticity was sharply peaked near an initial bias of -1; no numeric share is stated in the text.
rows.note: The paper says the preferred bias shifts slightly with learning rate.
rows.check: There is no numeric value in the text; the peak is read from Figure 13 only.

source_check.locator_found: Sec 4.1.2, Fig 13 text: peak near initial bias -1, shifts slightly with LR

rows.subject: random re-projector toy model
rows.operation_detail: Used negative initial mean bias and weight decay while varying learning rate.
rows.value: The authors report roughly one monosemantic neuron per feature across a range of learning rates.
rows.note: A separate toy task from the feature decoder.
rows.check: The paper gives no zero-bias baseline for the re-projector.

rows.subject: absolute value toy model
rows.operation_detail: Compared monosemanticity and task loss across training conditions and learning rates.
rows.value: More-monosemantic models had lower loss; a negative initial bias alone did not reliably produce mostly-monosemantic models. The paper reports that slower weight decay produced more monosemantic solutions.
rows.note: The result indicates task- and training-protocol dependence within the toy setting.
rows.check: Negative bias alone was insufficient; slower weight decay restored monosemanticity (Fig. 23). The row merges two findings, plus a loss–monosemanticity link that differs from the decoder task.

relationships.condition: Toy feature decoder, re-projector and absolute-value tasks with sparse features, under varied training path (learning rate, negative initial bias, bias weight decay; ReLU and GeLU)
relationships.reason: Models at equal loss range from mostly polysemantic to mostly monosemantic depending only on training choices (R1, R2, R5, R6). Polysemanticity was therefore not forced by capacity in these toy networks.
relationships.display_finding: At equal loss, models ranged from mostly polysemantic to mostly monosemantic depending only on training choices, so capacity did not force polysemanticity in these toy networks.

source_check.condition: Toy feature decoder, re-projector and absolute-value tasks with sparse features, under varied training path (learning rate, negative initial bias, bias weight decay; ReLU and GeLU)
source_check.reason: At equal loss, monosemanticity varies widely with LR, initial bias and decay (R1, R2, R5, R6). The absolute-value task also has LR-dependent basins (Fig 22), but there the losses differ.

relationships.condition: Toy decoder when width or feature density varies, and the absolute-value task
relationships.reason: Monosemantic count rises with width (R3), and dense features (Nε ≈ 2d) leave almost no monosemantic neurons whatever the training (R4). So capacity and the data distribution also set polysemanticity. Negative bias alone failed on the absolute-value task without slower decay (R7).
relationships.display_finding: The number of monosemantic neurons rose with width, and with dense features (Nε ≈ 2d) almost no neurons were monosemantic whatever the training, so capacity and the data distribution also set polysemanticity. On the absolute-value task, a negative bias alone failed without slower decay.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Toy decoder when width or feature density varies, and the absolute-value task
source_check.reason: The monosemantic count rises with width, and dense features force polysemanticity (R3, R4). The absolute-value task needs a high LR or slow decay on top of negative bias (R7). Negative bias still gives many monosemantic neurons at k<N, so the effect is qualified, not absent: not challenges.

source_check.notes: Code: Appendix A says the implementation is on GitHub, so the pack's 'code: n' is wrong. Table 1 is garbled (RG1/RP1/LR5/D1 columns misaligned). R1's LR 0.03 comes from Fig 4's highest LR1 panel and is not stated beside 503/512. The l0 reason ('equal loss') does not fit the absolute-value task, where more monosemantic models have lower loss.

statements.correction: 2211.09169 (Appendix A): 'An implementation of our model and training process is available on GitHub' (no link in the text). Preprint; loss serves as the capability check.
statements.problem: The 'why' says both studies are preprints without code. This study says its implementation is available on GitHub. The result claims for this study (503/512, 30-50%, GeLU, re-projector) are correct.

statements.correction: Absolute-value task (Sec 4, Sec 4.3, Figs 22-23): a negative initial bias alone does not robustly give mostly-monosemantic models. Either a high learning rate or a low weight-decay rate is also needed. Monosemanticity rises with LR at initial bias -1.
statements.problem: The absolute-value claim makes slower decay the only fix. The text says a high learning rate or a low weight-decay rate is needed in addition to negative bias.

statements.correction: Absolute-value task: a negative initial bias is insufficient on its own. Either slower weight decay or a high learning rate is also needed (Sec 4, Sec 4.3, Figs 22-23).
statements.problem: 'Negative bias alone fails without slower decay' leaves out that a high learning rate also works on the absolute-value task.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Negative-bias training in the tested toy networks
reader_labels.reason: Negative-bias training produced monosemantic solutions in the feature decoder and re-projector; see R2 and R6. These results support the narrower point that training choices can change monosemanticity, not the modern-architecture or tool-quality claims.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Feature-decoder width sweep in toy networks
reader_labels.reason: Increasing layer width increased the absolute number of monosemantic neurons, so the result challenges a strict ‘not capacity’ framing; however, the monosemantic fraction peaked rather than rising monotonically. See R3.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Changes in input feature frequency and task
reader_labels.reason: Monosemanticity depended on feature frequency and task: dense feature samples reduced it, and negative-bias training alone was insufficient for the absolute-value task. See R4 and R7.
